Anatolia.0: Hunter-gatherers raised the carved stone enclosures of Göbekli Tepe around 9500 BC, long before farming was fully established. Later Neolithic villagers grew wheat, herded animals and traded obsidian, and Çatalhöyük became one of the world's earliest large towns by c. 7400 BC. Copper working spread in the Chalcolithic age.
Anatolia.1: Early Bronze Age Anatolia was a land of fortified towns ruled by local chiefs, such as Troy on the Dardanelles and Alaca Höyük with its rich royal tombs. The Hattians lived in the central plateau, while Indo-European speakers, ancestors of the Hittites and Luwians, were settling in. Metalwork and long-distance trade grew steadily.
Anatolia.2: Assyrian merchants ran trading colonies at Kanesh around 1900 BC, bringing writing to Anatolia. From c. 1650 BC the Hittites built an empire from their capital Hattusa, rivaling Egypt and Mitanni. Around 1200 BC the Late Bronze Age collapse swept the empire away and Troy was destroyed, leaving smaller Neo-Hittite states.
Anatolia.3: After the Hittites fell, new kingdoms rose. Phrygia, ruled from Gordion by kings like Midas, dominated the center until Cimmerian raiders struck c. 700 BC, while Lydia grew rich at Sardis and minted the first coins c. 630 BC. Greeks settled the Aegean coast, and Urartu held the eastern highlands.
Anatolia.4: Lydia under Croesus reached its peak until Cyrus the Great conquered it in 547 BC, bringing Anatolia into the Persian Achaemenid Empire. Persian satraps ruled from Sardis, the start of the Royal Road to Susa. The Greek cities of Ionia, home of early philosophers like Thales of Miletus, now paid tribute to Persia.
Anatolia.5: The Ionian Greek cities rebelled against Persia in 499–493 BC, sparking the Greco-Persian Wars. After Persia's defeats in Greece, many coastal cities joined Athens' Delian League, while the interior stayed under Persian satraps. Herodotus, the first great historian, was born in Halicarnassus in this century.
Anatolia.6: Persia regained the Ionian coast in 387 BC, and local dynasts like Mausolus of Caria built grand monuments such as the Mausoleum. In 334 BC Alexander the Great crossed into Anatolia, won at the Granicus and swept east. After his death his generals fought over the region, notably at Ipsus in 301 BC.
Anatolia.7: Anatolia split among Hellenistic powers. The Seleucids held much of it, while the Attalid kings made Pergamon a brilliant center of art and learning. Celtic Galatians invaded in 278 BC and settled the central plateau, and native kingdoms such as Bithynia, Pontus and Cappadocia grew in strength.
Anatolia.8: Rome defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC and handed much of Anatolia to its ally Pergamon. When Attalus III died in 133 BC he bequeathed Pergamon to Rome, which formed the province of Asia. Roman tax collectors arrived, and the kingdom of Pontus began to rise.
Anatolia.9: Mithridates VI of Pontus challenged Rome in the Mithridatic Wars of 88–63 BC, at first massacring Romans across Asia. Sulla, Lucullus and finally Pompey defeated him and reorganized Anatolia into Roman provinces and client kingdoms. Caesar won quickly at Zela in 47 BC, and Augustus added Galatia in 25 BC.
Anatolia.10: Under the Roman peace, Anatolian cities like Ephesus, Smyrna and Pergamon flourished with theaters, baths and trade. The apostle Paul, from Tarsus, spread Christianity through the region, and early churches took root in many towns. Rome annexed Cappadocia in AD 17, tightening its hold on the interior.
Anatolia.11: The 100s were a golden age for Roman Anatolia. Emperors like Hadrian funded grand buildings, the Library of Celsus rose at Ephesus, and Greek orators and the physician Galen of Pergamon won fame. Christianity kept spreading, though the Antonine Plague of the 160s struck the population hard.
Anatolia.12: Rome's third-century crisis reached Anatolia as Gothic raiders plundered the coasts and burned the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus. Persian armies under Shapur I raided the east, and Zenobia of Palmyra briefly seized parts of the region. Diocletian restored order from 284, ruling from Nicomedia.
Anatolia.13: Constantine founded Constantinople in 330 on the Bosporus, making Anatolia the heartland of a new Christian Roman state. The Council of Nicaea in 325 defined Christian doctrine, and Cappadocian bishops like Basil shaped theology. By the 380s Christianity was the official religion and pagan temples declined.
Anatolia.14: While the western Roman Empire collapsed, the eastern or Byzantine Empire held firm, with Anatolia as its secure core of farms, cities and soldiers. Church councils at Ephesus in 431 and Chalcedon in 451 debated the nature of Christ. Isaurian highlanders gained power, and one, Zeno, became emperor.
Anatolia.15: Under Justinian the Byzantine Empire built Hagia Sophia and tried to reconquer the West. Anatolia supplied taxes and troops but suffered the Plague of Justinian from 541, which killed a large share of the population. Wars with Sasanian Persia flared repeatedly along the eastern frontier.
Anatolia.16: Persian armies overran Anatolia during the war of 602–628, reaching the Bosporus. Soon after, Arab Muslim armies began yearly raids and besieged Constantinople in 674–678. The Byzantines reorganized Anatolia into military districts called themes, and many cities shrank into fortified hilltop towns.
Anatolia.17: Leo III defeated the great Arab siege of Constantinople in 717–718, and Byzantine troops won at Akroinon in 740, securing Anatolia. Emperors began Iconoclasm, banning religious images, which divided the church until the Council of Nicaea in 787 restored them. Arab border raids continued each summer.
Anatolia.18: Abbasid armies sacked the Anatolian city of Amorion in 838, but Byzantium steadily recovered. Icon veneration was permanently restored in 843, and the heretical Paulician state in the east was crushed in 872. The Macedonian dynasty, from 867, began pushing the frontier back eastward.
Anatolia.19: The Byzantine Empire went on the offensive, retaking Melitene and in 969 Antioch under soldier-emperors like Nikephoros Phokas and John Tzimiskes. Great Anatolian landowning families grew powerful and sometimes rebelled. Basil II, crowned in 976, would lead the empire to a new peak.
Anatolia.20: Byzantium annexed Armenian lands early in the century, but Seljuk Turks raided deeper and won a crushing victory at Manzikert in 1071. Turkish groups settled much of the plateau, founding the Sultanate of Rum. The First Crusade crossed Anatolia in 1097, helping the Komnenos emperors regain the western coast.
Anatolia.21: The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, ruling from Konya, controlled central Anatolia and competed with the Danishmendid Turks and the Byzantines on the coasts. Byzantium lost a major battle at Myriokephalon in 1176. Armenians built a kingdom in Cilicia, and Crusaders kept marching through, with Frederick Barbarossa drowning there in 1190.
Anatolia.22: Rum prospered early in the century, building caravanserais along trade roads, and the poet Rumi taught in Konya. The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, leaving Greek successor states at Nicaea and Trebizond. After the Mongols made Rum a vassal in 1243, small Turkish emirates emerged, including Osman's c. 1299.
Anatolia.23: The Ottomans grew from a frontier emirate into a major power, taking Bursa in 1326, Nicaea in 1331 and crossing into Europe at Gallipoli in 1354. They moved their capital to Edirne and won in the Balkans at Kosovo in 1389. Bayezid I then absorbed rival Turkish emirates across Anatolia.
Anatolia.24: Timur crushed Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402, triggering an Ottoman civil war until 1413. The state recovered, and in 1453 Mehmed II conquered Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire and making Istanbul his capital. Trebizond and the emirate of Karaman were absorbed, uniting Anatolia under Ottoman rule.
Anatolia.25: Selim I defeated Safavid Iran at Chaldiran in 1514 and conquered the Mamluks in 1516–17, making the Ottomans masters of the Arab heartlands. Under Suleiman the Magnificent, 1520–66, the empire peaked, and the architect Sinan built great mosques. Late in the century the Celali revolts shook rural Anatolia.
Anatolia.26: Rural unrest, inflation and palace intrigue weakened the Ottoman state early in the century. The Köprülü family of grand viziers restored order from 1656, but the failed siege of Vienna in 1683 began a long retreat. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 brought the first major territorial losses in Europe.
Anatolia.27: Istanbul's elite enjoyed the Tulip Era of 1718–30, with gardens, palaces and the first Ottoman Muslim printing press, until the Patrona Halil revolt ended it. Wars with Russia and Austria continued, though the Ottomans regained Belgrade in 1739. Provincial notables increasingly controlled Anatolian towns.
Anatolia.28: Defeat by Russia in 1768–74 ended with the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, and Russia annexed Crimea in 1783. Local notables called ayans held real power across Anatolia. Selim III, sultan from 1789, launched the New Order reforms to build a modern army, angering the Janissaries.
Anatolia.29: Selim III was overthrown in 1807 by conservative Janissaries, and Mahmud II took the throne in 1808, slowly rebuilding central authority. The empire faced national revolts in the Balkans, first in Serbia from 1804 and then the Greek War of Independence from 1821.
Anatolia.30: Mahmud II destroyed the Janissary corps in 1826 and built a modern army. Greece won independence in 1830, and the Egyptian forces of Muhammad Ali invaded Anatolia, reaching Konya in 1832. In 1839 the Tanzimat reforms began, promising equal rights and modern administration for all subjects.
Anatolia.31: Britain and France helped the Ottomans defeat Russia in the Crimean War of 1853–56, yet the empire was increasingly called the 'sick man of Europe'. The 1856 reform edict expanded equality for non-Muslims. Hundreds of thousands of Circassian refugees from Russia settled in Anatolia, and foreign debt mounted.
Anatolia.32: The Ottoman state went bankrupt in 1875, and in 1876 it adopted its first constitution. Abdulhamid II suspended parliament after losing the 1877–78 war with Russia and ruled as an autocrat, building railways and schools. European creditors took over parts of the finances, and massacres of Armenians in 1894–96 killed tens of thousands or more.
Anatolia.33: The Young Turk Revolution of 1908 restored the constitution, and Abdulhamid II was deposed in 1909. The Committee of Union and Progress rose to power. In 1908 Austria annexed Bosnia and Bulgaria declared full independence, and the 1909 Adana massacre killed thousands of Armenians, showing rising ethnic tension.
Anatolia.34: The Ottomans lost most of their Balkan lands in 1912–13 and entered World War I on Germany's side. They won at Gallipoli in 1915, but the government carried out the Armenian genocide, also killing many Assyrians and Greeks. After defeat in 1918, Mustafa Kemal led the Turkish War of Independence.
Anatolia.35: Turkish forces defeated Greece in 1922, and the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 recognized the new Republic of Turkey under Atatürk, with Ankara as capital. Greece and Turkey exchanged populations. The caliphate was abolished in 1924, and sweeping secular reforms introduced Western law and the Latin alphabet.
Anatolia.36: Atatürk's one-party republic pushed modernization further: women gained the vote in 1934, citizens took surnames, and the state built factories. A Kurdish uprising in Dersim was harshly suppressed in 1937–38. Atatürk died in 1938, succeeded by İsmet İnönü, and Turkey gained Hatay from French Syria in 1939.
Anatolia.37: Turkey stayed neutral through most of World War II, joining the Allies only in 1945. A 1942 wealth tax fell heavily on non-Muslim citizens. After the war, Soviet pressure pushed Turkey toward the United States, which sent aid from 1947, and multiparty politics began in 1946.
Anatolia.38: The Democrat Party under Adnan Menderes won the 1950 election, ending one-party rule. Turkey sent troops to Korea and joined NATO in 1952. Farms mechanized and villagers flooded into cities, but debt and repression grew, and the 1955 Istanbul riots targeted the Greek community.
Anatolia.39: The army overthrew Menderes in 1960 and executed him in 1961, then introduced a more liberal constitution. Hundreds of thousands of Turkish workers began moving to West Germany and other European countries. Politics became polarized between left and right, and crises in Cyprus strained relations with Greece.
Anatolia.40: The military forced out the government in 1971, and Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 after a Greek-backed coup there, dividing the island. Economic crisis and street violence between leftists and nationalists killed thousands. The Kurdish militant group PKK was founded in 1978.
Anatolia.41: The army seized power in 1980 and imposed a new constitution in 1982. Turgut Özal then opened the economy to markets and exports. The PKK began an armed insurgency in the Kurdish southeast in 1984, a conflict that would last decades, and Turkey applied to join the European Community in 1987.
Anatolia.42: The war with the PKK peaked, displacing many Kurdish villagers, until leader Abdullah Öcalan was captured in 1999. The Islamist Welfare Party briefly led the government before military pressure forced it out in 1997. The İzmit earthquake of 1999 killed about 17,000, and Turkey became an EU candidate.
Anatolia.43: After a severe financial crisis in 2001, the AKP led by Recep Tayyip Erdoğan won power in 2002. Turkey enjoyed rapid growth, passed reforms and opened EU membership talks in 2005. Tensions grew between the governing party and the secular establishment, including the army.
Anatolia.44: Mass Gezi Park protests in 2013 challenged Erdoğan's rule, and Turkey took in several million Syrian refugees. Peace talks with the PKK collapsed in 2015. After a failed coup in 2016, the government purged tens of thousands, and a 2017 referendum created a powerful executive presidency.
Anatolia.45: Turkey faced high inflation and a currency slide. Earthquakes in February 2023 killed over 50,000 people in the southeast. Erdoğan won reelection in 2023, the 2025 arrest of Istanbul's opposition mayor sparked large protests, and the PKK announced in 2025 that it would disband.

Israel.0: Natufian hunter-gatherers built some of the first permanent villages here, and by c. 9000 BC Jericho had become one of the world's oldest towns, later ringed by a stone wall and tower. Farming and herding spread through the Neolithic, and later Chalcolithic villagers made fine copperwork.
Israel.1: Early Bronze Age Canaanites built walled towns such as Megiddo and Arad, growing olives, grapes and grain and trading with Egypt. Around 2300 BC many towns were abandoned, and for a few centuries people lived mainly in villages and as pastoral herders.
Israel.2: Canaanite city-states revived and grew rich, then came under Egyptian control in the New Kingdom, as the Amarna letters show. After the Bronze Age collapse c. 1200 BC, Philistines settled the coast and Israelites emerged in the hill country, first named on an Egyptian stele c. 1208 BC.
Israel.3: Tradition credits David and Solomon with a united kingdom c. 1000 BC, though historians debate its size. The northern Kingdom of Israel, capital Samaria, was destroyed by Assyria in 722 BC, while Judah, centered on Jerusalem, survived as a vassal. Prophets and royal reforms shaped Israelite religion.
Israel.4: Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple in 586 BC and deported much of Judah's elite. After Cyrus of Persia took Babylon, he allowed Jews to return in 538 BC, and the Second Temple was completed in 516 BC. Judah became the small Persian province of Yehud.
Israel.5: Yehud remained a modest Persian province centered on the rebuilt Temple. Leaders like Nehemiah restored Jerusalem's walls around 445 BC, and Ezra promoted Torah observance. Scribes were shaping the Hebrew scriptures, while Samaritans to the north developed their own tradition.
Israel.6: Alexander the Great took the region in 332 BC after besieging Tyre and Gaza. After his death it passed to the Ptolemies of Egypt from 301 BC. Greek-style cities, coins and culture began to spread, slowly influencing local Jewish life.
Israel.7: The Ptolemies ruled from Alexandria, taxing the land through local agents, while Jewish scholars in Egypt began translating the Torah into Greek. Ptolemaic and Seleucid kings fought repeated wars over the region, and in 200 BC the Seleucid Antiochus III won it at Panium.
Israel.8: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV banned Jewish practices and desecrated the Temple, sparking the Maccabean revolt of 167–160 BC. The Temple's rededication is remembered at Hanukkah. The Hasmonean family then built an independent Jewish kingdom that expanded its borders.
Israel.9: Hasmonean rivals called in Rome, and Pompey took Judea in 63 BC. Rome made Herod the Great king in 37 BC, and he rebuilt the Temple on a grand scale and founded Caesarea. Jesus of Nazareth was born c. 4 BC, near the end of Herod's reign.
Israel.10: Roman governors ruled Judea, and Jesus was crucified c. 30–33, after which his followers spread Christianity. Tensions with Rome exploded in the Jewish revolt of 66–73, and the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70. Rabbinic Judaism began to take shape without the Temple.
Israel.11: The Bar Kokhba revolt of 132–136 ended in massive destruction, and Hadrian rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan colony, barring Jews from the city. Rome renamed the province Syria Palaestina. Jewish life shifted to Galilee, where rabbis compiled the Mishnah around 200.
Israel.12: Jewish scholars in Galilee built on the Mishnah, and synagogues were common in the region. Caesarea became a center of Christian learning under the scholar Origen. The region shared in the Roman Empire's third-century turmoil but stayed relatively stable.
Israel.13: After Constantine's conversion the land became the Christian Holy Land, with the Church of the Holy Sepulchre built in Jerusalem in the 330s. Pilgrims arrived from across the empire. Emperor Julian's plan to rebuild the Jewish Temple in 363 failed, and the Jerusalem Talmud was completed around 400.
Israel.14: Under Byzantine rule, the region was split into three provinces of Palaestina and grew prosperous and populous. Monasteries filled the Judean desert, and Jerusalem became a patriarchate in 451. Jewish and Samaritan communities continued, though under increasing legal restrictions.
Israel.15: Samaritan revolts against Byzantine rule were crushed in 529 and 556. Justinian built the great Nea Church in Jerusalem, and churches with fine mosaics, like the one recorded on the Madaba Map, dotted the land. The plague of 541 brought heavy losses.
Israel.16: Sasanian Persia captured Jerusalem in 614, Byzantium returned briefly, and Arab Muslim armies took the city in 637 under Caliph Umar. Under Umayyad rule the Dome of the Rock was finished in 691. Christians and Jews remained, while Arabic and Islam slowly spread.
Israel.17: The Umayyads built the al-Aqsa Mosque and founded Ramla as the capital of the province of Filastin. A major earthquake in 749 devastated towns like Beit She'an. In 750 the Abbasids took over, shifting power to distant Iraq, and the region became a quieter province.
Israel.18: Under the Abbasids and then, from 878, the Tulunids of Egypt, the region was a provincial backwater, but Jerusalem remained a pilgrimage site for Muslims, Christians and Jews. Arabic became the common language, and more of the population gradually converted to Islam.
Israel.19: Egyptian dynasties, first the Ikhshidids and then from the 970s the Shia Fatimids, contested control with Bedouin and Qarmatian raiders. In Tiberias, Jewish scholars called the Masoretes perfected the Hebrew Bible's text, producing manuscripts like the Aleppo Codex.
Israel.20: The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim destroyed the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009, and Seljuk Turks took Jerusalem in 1073. Crusaders captured the city in 1099, massacring many inhabitants, and founded the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, ruled by European knights.
Israel.21: The Crusader kingdom built castles and relied on military orders like the Templars and Hospitallers. Saladin destroyed its army at Hattin in 1187 and retook Jerusalem. The Third Crusade under Richard the Lionheart regained the coast, leaving a smaller kingdom based at Acre.
Israel.22: Frederick II briefly regained Jerusalem by treaty in 1229, but it was lost for good in 1244. The Mamluk sultans of Egypt, led by Baybars, took Crusader castles one by one, and the fall of Acre in 1291 ended the Crusader states. Mamluks then ruled the region.
Israel.23: The Mamluks governed the land as provinces under Damascus and Cairo, endowing religious schools and hostels in Jerusalem. The Black Death of 1348 cut the population. Franciscan friars became custodians of Christian holy sites, and Jewish communities persisted in towns like Jerusalem.
Israel.24: Under late Mamluk rule the region was poor and thinly populated, troubled by plague, heavy taxes and Bedouin raids. After the expulsion of Jews from Spain in 1492, some Sephardic Jews began to settle here, especially in Safed and Jerusalem.
Israel.25: The Ottomans conquered the land in 1516, beginning four centuries of rule. Suleiman the Magnificent built Jerusalem's still-standing walls in 1537–41. Safed became a thriving center of Jewish mysticism and law, home to scholars like Isaac Luria and Joseph Karo.
Israel.26: Ottoman governors under Damascus ruled loosely, and the Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II controlled Galilee early in the century. In 1665 the self-proclaimed messiah Sabbatai Zevi was declared in Gaza, stirring Jewish communities worldwide. Local economies and towns declined.
Israel.27: Local strongmen gained power under loose Ottoman rule. Zahir al-Umar, an Arab chief, began building an autonomous domain in Galilee from the 1730s, based first at Tiberias and growing rich on cotton exports. Small groups of Jewish pilgrims settled in Jerusalem.
Israel.28: Zahir al-Umar ruled Galilee from Acre until he was killed in 1775, and the ruthless governor Jazzar Pasha took over. In 1799 Napoleon invaded from Egypt but failed to capture Acre. Hasidic Jews from Eastern Europe settled in Galilee from 1777.
Israel.29: After Jazzar's death in 1804, governors at Acre continued to dominate the region under nominal Ottoman rule. Disciples of the Vilna Gaon settled in Safed and Jerusalem. Most inhabitants were Arab Muslim and Christian villagers, with small Jewish communities in the holy cities.
Israel.30: Egypt's Ibrahim Pasha ruled the region from 1831 to 1840, introducing conscription and reforms and crushing a peasant revolt in 1834. An earthquake devastated Safed in 1837. European powers opened consulates, and Ottoman rule returned in 1840 with European help.
Israel.31: Ottoman Tanzimat reforms reshaped land ownership and administration. Disputes over Christian holy places helped trigger the Crimean War. Jerusalem began expanding beyond its walls in the 1860s, and missionaries, pilgrims and German Templer colonists added to a growing European presence.
Israel.32: Most of the population were Arab Muslims and Christians, while Jaffa and Jerusalem grew. In 1882 the First Aliyah brought Jewish immigrants from Russia and Romania, founding farm colonies supported by Baron Rothschild. In 1897 Theodor Herzl launched political Zionism at the First Zionist Congress.
Israel.33: The Second Aliyah from 1904 brought socialist Zionist pioneers who founded the first kibbutz at Degania in 1909, the same year Tel Aviv was founded. Arab newspapers and leaders began voicing concern about land sales and immigration. The 1908 Young Turk Revolution briefly raised hopes for reform.
Israel.34: World War I brought hunger, locusts and Ottoman repression. In 1917 Britain issued the Balfour Declaration, supporting a Jewish national home while promising to protect the rights of non-Jewish communities, and British forces took Jerusalem in December. Both Arab and Jewish national movements grew.
Israel.35: Britain governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate. Jewish immigration and institutions expanded, including the Hebrew University in 1925. Arab Palestinians opposed the mandate's Zionist commitments, and violence erupted in 1920, 1921 and 1929, when the Jewish community of Hebron was attacked.
Israel.36: Nazi persecution drove a large wave of Jewish immigration. Palestinian Arabs launched a revolt in 1936–39, which Britain suppressed. The Peel Commission proposed partition in 1937, and the 1939 White Paper sharply limited Jewish immigration.
Israel.37: After World War II and the Holocaust, Jewish groups fought British rule. The UN proposed partition in 1947, civil war followed, and Israel declared independence in 1948. Arab states invaded, and about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled (the Nakba). Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt Gaza.
Israel.38: Israel's population roughly doubled as Holocaust survivors and Jews from Arab countries arrived. Palestinian refugees lived in camps in neighboring lands and Gaza. Israel joined Britain and France in the 1956 Suez War, and Palestinian activists founded Fatah in 1959.
Israel.39: Israel tried Nazi official Adolf Eichmann in 1961, and Arab states created the PLO in 1964. In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel captured the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai, Golan Heights and East Jerusalem. Military occupation and the first settlements followed.
Israel.40: Egypt and Syria attacked in the 1973 Yom Kippur War, and Israel prevailed at heavy cost. The right-wing Likud won power in 1977, and Egypt's Sadat visited Jerusalem, leading to the 1979 peace treaty. Settlements in the occupied territories expanded.
Israel.41: Israel returned Sinai to Egypt by 1982 and invaded Lebanon to expel the PLO. Ethiopian Jews were airlifted to Israel. In 1987 the First Intifada, a mass Palestinian uprising, erupted in the occupied territories, and Hamas was founded the same year.
Israel.42: Around a million immigrants arrived from the former Soviet Union. The 1993 Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority and a path to negotiations, and Israel made peace with Jordan in 1994. A Jewish extremist assassinated Prime Minister Rabin in 1995, and attacks and settlement growth eroded the process.
Israel.43: Peace talks failed in 2000, and the Second Intifada brought suicide bombings and Israeli military operations, killing thousands. Israel built a separation barrier and withdrew from Gaza in 2005. Hamas won Palestinian elections and seized Gaza in 2007, followed by a blockade and wars.
Israel.44: Israel's tech economy boomed and offshore gas was found, while Benjamin Netanyahu led long governments. Wars with Hamas in Gaza in 2012 and 2014 killed many civilians, mostly Palestinians. The US moved its embassy to Jerusalem in 2018, and peace talks stayed frozen.
Israel.45: Israel normalized ties with the UAE and others in 2020, and a judicial overhaul sparked mass protests in 2023. Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack killed about 1,200 people and took 250 hostages, and Israel's war in Gaza killed tens of thousands and caused a humanitarian catastrophe before a ceasefire in October 2025.

Levant.0: The Levant was one of the birthplaces of farming. Natufian foragers settled in villages, and by c. 9000 BC people at sites like Abu Hureyra and Tell Aswad were cultivating cereals. Later Neolithic towns such as Ain Ghazal made plaster statues, and Byblos began its long life as a settlement.
Levant.1: Early Bronze Age cities grew wealthy on trade. Ebla in Syria kept vast clay archives around 2400 BC, and Mari on the Euphrates was a major center. Byblos shipped cedar to Egypt, and Akkadian kings from Mesopotamia raided the region. Amorite peoples became prominent near the end.
Levant.2: Amorite kingdoms like Yamhad at Aleppo flourished, and Ugarit became a great trading port that used an early alphabet. Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites competed for control, fighting at Kadesh in 1274 BC before signing a peace treaty. Around 1200 BC the Bronze Age collapse destroyed Ugarit, and Arameans spread.
Levant.3: Aramean kingdoms, especially Damascus, ruled inland Syria, while Phoenician cities like Tyre and Sidon spread trade and their alphabet across the Mediterranean, founding Carthage in 814 BC. Ammon, Moab and Edom held Jordan. Assyria conquered the region in the 700s BC, later followed by Babylon.
Levant.4: Babylon's Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for 13 years and dominated the region until Persia took over after 539 BC. Under the Achaemenids, the Levant became the satrapy of 'Beyond the River'. Phoenician cities kept their kings and supplied Persia's navy.
Levant.5: Persian rule was mostly stable. Phoenician kings in Sidon, Tyre and Byblos governed their cities, minted coins and sent fleets against Greece. Aramaic served as the common administrative language, and Arab peoples controlled the desert trade routes to the south and east.
Levant.6: Persia crushed a revolt at Sidon in 351 BC. Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus in 333 BC and took Tyre after a long siege. After his death, Seleucus founded his empire in 312 BC and built new Greek cities like Antioch and Apamea, while the Nabataeans grew rich at Petra.
Levant.7: The Seleucids of Antioch and the Ptolemies of Egypt fought repeated Syrian Wars over the region, with the south under Ptolemaic rule. Greek-style cities, temples and theaters spread. In 200 BC Antiochus III won the whole Levant for the Seleucids at Panium.
Levant.8: After Rome defeated Antiochus III in 190 BC, the Seleucid kingdom weakened through civil wars among rival kings. Local powers took advantage: the Hasmoneans in Judea, Nabataean Arabs in the south and Iturean chiefs in Lebanon all expanded, while Parthia pressed from the east.
Levant.9: Armenia's Tigranes the Great briefly ruled Syria until Pompey made it a Roman province in 64 BC, with Antioch as its capital. Parthians invaded in 40 BC but were driven out. The Nabataean kingdom of Petra was at its height, controlling incense caravan routes.
Levant.10: Roman Syria prospered, and caravan cities like Palmyra grew wealthy on trade with the East. Christianity spread early, and followers were first called Christians at Antioch. Huge temples rose at Baalbek, and Greek cities of the Decapolis such as Gerasa flourished.
Levant.11: Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 as the province of Arabia and built a new road from Bosra to the Red Sea. Palmyra reached its peak as a trading hub. Cities across Syria built colonnaded streets and temples during this prosperous Roman century.
Levant.12: Syrians reached the top of Roman power: Julia Domna of Emesa became empress, and Philip the Arab was emperor in 244–249. Persia's Shapur I sacked Antioch, and Queen Zenobia of Palmyra briefly ruled the Roman East in 267–272 before Aurelian crushed her and destroyed Palmyra.
Levant.13: Christianity became the dominant faith as the empire converted, and Antioch was one of its great centers, home to preachers like John Chrysostom. Syriac-speaking writers such as Ephrem enriched Christian literature. The eastern frontier saw repeated wars with Sasanian Persia.
Levant.14: Under Byzantine rule the countryside thrived with olive-growing villages, now the 'Dead Cities' of northern Syria. Simeon Stylites drew pilgrims to his pillar near Aleppo. After the Council of Chalcedon in 451, many Syriac Christians split from the imperial church.
Levant.15: The Ghassanid Arabs guarded Byzantium's desert frontier. Disasters struck: earthquakes ruined Antioch in 526 and Beirut in 551, Persia's Khosrow I sacked Antioch in 540, and plague arrived in 541. Jacob Baradaeus organized the Syriac Orthodox Church.
Levant.16: Persia occupied the Levant in 611–628, and soon after, Arab Muslim armies won at Yarmouk in 636. Muawiya governed Syria and became the first Umayyad caliph in 661, making Damascus the capital of an empire from Spain to Central Asia. Christians remained the majority for some time.
Levant.17: The Umayyads built the Great Mosque of Damascus and desert palaces in Syria and Jordan. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew them and moved the capital to Iraq, and Syria lost its central role. Arabic spread as the language of government.
Levant.18: Syria was a province of the Abbasid caliphate, often restless under distant rule. In 878 the Tulunids of Egypt took control. Arabic was steadily replacing Aramaic and Greek in daily life, and the share of Muslims in the population grew.
Levant.19: The Hamdanid prince Sayf al-Dawla ruled Aleppo as a brilliant court, home to the poet al-Mutanabbi. Byzantium retook Antioch in 969, and the Fatimids of Egypt seized Damascus in the 970s. The Levant became a contested frontier between empires.
Levant.20: Fatimids, Byzantines and local Arab dynasties competed for Syria, and the Druze faith emerged in the mountains. Seljuk Turks took Damascus in 1076. The First Crusade captured Antioch in 1098 and founded Crusader states including the County of Tripoli.
Levant.21: Muslim leaders united against the Crusaders. Zengi took Edessa in 1144, Nur al-Din unified Syria, and Saladin, founder of the Ayyubid dynasty, retook most of the Levant after Hattin in 1187. Crusaders held coastal cities and castles like Krak des Chevaliers.
Levant.22: Ayyubid princes ruled Syrian cities. The Mongols took Aleppo and Damascus in 1260, but the Mamluks of Egypt defeated them at Ain Jalut that year. Sultan Baybars then captured Antioch and other Crusader strongholds, and Acre's fall in 1291 ended the Crusades.
Levant.23: The Mamluks ruled Syria from Cairo, repelling Mongol invasions in 1299–1303. Damascus and Aleppo flourished with mosques, schools and markets, and scholars like Ibn Taymiyya taught there. The Black Death in 1348 killed many people. Timur's armies approached at the century's end.
Levant.24: Timur sacked Aleppo and Damascus in 1400–01, carrying off artisans to Samarkand. The Mamluks slowly restored their rule, and Syrian cities rebuilt. Trade with Venice and other Italian cities through Beirut and Aleppo kept the economy going.
Levant.25: The Ottomans defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and ruled Syria from Istanbul. Damascus organized the great hajj caravan to Mecca, and Aleppo became a major hub of silk and spice trade with European merchants. Druze emirs governed Mount Lebanon.
Levant.26: The Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II built a semi-independent state in Lebanon and northern Palestine until the Ottomans executed him in 1635. English and French merchants traded in Aleppo, and Ottoman governors struggled with local factions and Janissary garrisons.
Levant.27: The Shihab family led Mount Lebanon from 1697, and the al-Azm family governed Damascus, building the Azm Palace. In 1724 a split in the Antiochian Orthodox church created the Melkite Greek Catholic Church. Ottoman authority was increasingly delegated to local families.
Levant.28: Local strongmen like Zahir al-Umar and later Jazzar Pasha in Acre dominated parts of the Levant. A strong earthquake struck in 1759. Bashir II Shihab rose to power in Mount Lebanon in 1789, and Napoleon's 1799 invasion was halted at Acre.
Levant.29: Bashir II Shihab ruled Mount Lebanon with growing power, while Ottoman governors in Damascus and Aleppo faced Wahhabi raids from Arabia. Aleppo suffered a devastating earthquake in 1822. Central Ottoman control remained weak, and local families and governors ran most daily affairs.
Levant.30: Egypt's Ibrahim Pasha conquered Syria in 1831–32 and ruled until 1840, introducing conscription and modern administration but provoking revolts. European powers forced Egypt out and restored the Ottomans. Bashir II was exiled, and Druze-Maronite tensions rose in Mount Lebanon.
Levant.31: Civil war between Druze and Maronites in Mount Lebanon in 1860 and a massacre of Christians in Damascus brought French intervention. Mount Lebanon became an autonomous district under a Christian governor in 1861. Beirut grew into a port, and missionaries founded schools like the Syrian Protestant College in 1866.
Levant.32: Beirut became a center of the Arab cultural revival called the Nahda, with presses, newspapers and schools. The Beirut-Damascus railway opened in 1895. Large numbers of Syrians and Lebanese, especially Christians, began emigrating to the Americas.
Levant.33: The Hejaz Railway linked Damascus to Medina by 1908, partly to carry pilgrims. The Young Turk Revolution of 1908 brought elections and new freedoms, but growing Turkish centralization pushed Arab intellectuals to form nationalist societies.
Levant.34: World War I brought famine that killed a large share of Mount Lebanon's people, and Ottoman governor Jamal Pasha hanged Arab nationalists in 1916. Britain and France secretly divided the region in the Sykes-Picot Agreement. The Arab Revolt and British forces drove out the Ottomans in 1918.
Levant.35: Faisal proclaimed an Arab Kingdom of Syria in 1920, but France crushed it at Maysalun and took mandates over Syria and Greater Lebanon. Britain set up the Emirate of Transjordan under Abdullah in 1921. A Great Syrian Revolt against French rule in 1925–27 was suppressed.
Levant.36: Syrian and Lebanese nationalists pressed France for independence, winning a 1936 treaty that France never ratified. Turkey annexed the Syrian province of Alexandretta, now Hatay, in 1939. Transjordan developed under British guidance, and Lebanon's Christian and Muslim elites negotiated a shared vision of independence.
Levant.37: Allied forces took Syria and Lebanon from Vichy France in 1941. Lebanon became independent in 1943 under a power-sharing National Pact, Syria in 1946, and Jordan in 1946. The 1948 war brought Palestinian refugees to all three, and Syria suffered its first military coup in 1949.
Levant.38: Jordan's King Abdullah was assassinated in 1951, and Hussein became king in 1953. Syria saw repeated coups and the rise of the Ba'ath Party, then merged with Egypt in the United Arab Republic in 1958. That year a crisis in Lebanon drew in US Marines.
Levant.39: Syria left the union with Egypt in 1961, and the Ba'ath Party seized power in 1963. In 1967 Israel took the Golan Heights from Syria and the West Bank from Jordan. Beirut boomed as a banking and cultural capital, and Palestinian militant groups grew.
Levant.40: Jordan expelled Palestinian guerrillas in Black September in 1970, and many moved to Lebanon. Hafez al-Assad seized power in Syria that year. After the 1973 war, Lebanon's tensions exploded into civil war in 1975, and Syrian troops entered in 1976.
Levant.41: Assad's forces crushed an uprising at Hama in 1982, killing thousands. Israel invaded Lebanon that year, and the Shia militia Hezbollah emerged with Iranian support. Bombings struck Western forces in Beirut in 1983, and the Taif Agreement of 1989 set terms to end Lebanon's war.
Levant.42: Lebanon's civil war ended in 1990, and Rafik Hariri led reconstruction under Syrian dominance. Jordan signed peace with Israel in 1994. King Hussein died in 1999 and was succeeded by Abdullah II, while Hafez al-Assad ruled Syria until 2000.
Levant.43: Bashar al-Assad succeeded his father in 2000, and Israel withdrew from southern Lebanon. The 2005 assassination of Rafik Hariri sparked protests that forced Syrian troops out of Lebanon. Israel and Hezbollah fought a war in 2006, and Iraqi refugees poured into Syria and Jordan.
Levant.44: Peaceful protests in Syria in 2011 turned into a brutal civil war, killing hundreds of thousands and displacing millions to Lebanon, Jordan and beyond. ISIS declared a 'caliphate' in 2014 before its defeat by 2019, and Russia and Iran helped Assad survive. Lebanon's economy collapsed in 2019.
Levant.45: A huge explosion devastated Beirut's port in 2020 amid Lebanon's financial crisis. Israel and Hezbollah fought an escalating war in 2024. In December 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham toppled the Assad regime, and Syria's new government faced the challenge of rebuilding a divided country.

Arabia.0: During wetter 'Green Arabia' phases, lakes and grasslands drew early human hunters across the peninsula. In the Neolithic, cattle and goat herders left rock art and built large stone monuments called mustatils. By c. 5000 BC fishing communities on the Gulf coast traded with Mesopotamia's Ubaid culture.
Arabia.1: Dilmun, centered on Bahrain, became a trading hub linking Mesopotamia with the Indus Valley, while Magan in Oman mined copper. Oasis farmers grew date palms, and the Umm an-Nar culture built round stone tombs. Most of the interior remained home to mobile herders.
Arabia.2: Dilmun continued to thrive on Gulf trade, and in Oman the Wadi Suq culture lived in oasis villages. Late in this period the camel was domesticated, opening the deserts to long-distance travel. Early frankincense and myrrh trading from the south began to take shape.
Arabia.3: Camel caravans carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean. The Kingdom of Saba (Sheba) in Yemen grew rich on this trade and built the great Marib dam. Oasis towns like Dedan and Tayma flourished, and Assyrian records mention Arab queens and tribes.
Arabia.4: The Babylonian king Nabonidus lived for about ten years at the oasis of Tayma in northwest Arabia, c. 552–543 BC. In the south, kingdoms such as Saba, Qataban, Hadramawt and Ma'in prospered from incense. The Lihyanite kingdom rose at Dedan along the caravan road.
Arabia.5: Greek writers like Herodotus marveled at Arabian spices. Minaean merchants from Yemen ran caravans north, and Gerrha on the Gulf coast grew rich in trade. Most Arabians lived as Bedouin herders or oasis farmers, organized by tribe.
Arabia.6: Alexander the Great was planning an Arabian campaign when he died in 323 BC. The Gulf trading city of Gerrha prospered, Nabataean Arabs grew powerful in the northwest, and the South Arabian kingdoms continued to profit from the incense routes.
Arabia.7: The South Arabian kingdoms of Saba, Qataban, Hadramawt and Ma'in shared the incense trade, building temples and irrigation works. In 205 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus III sailed to Gerrha and accepted tribute in silver and spices. Nabataean caravans dominated the northern routes.
Arabia.8: Himyar emerged in the highlands of Yemen around 110 BC. Greek sailors began using the monsoon winds to sail to India, slowly shifting trade from camel caravans to sea routes. Nabataeans expanded their control of oases in the northwest.
Arabia.9: Rome sent Aelius Gallus to conquer southern Arabia in 26–25 BC, but the expedition failed in the desert. The Nabataeans built monumental tombs at Hegra, and Himyar grew in power in Yemen. Incense remained Arabia's most famous export.
Arabia.10: Red Sea and Indian Ocean shipping boomed, as described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, reducing the importance of overland caravans. Nabataean Hegra carved its finest tombs. In Yemen, Himyar and Saba vied for power as Qataban faded.
Arabia.11: Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106, stationing troops as far as Hegra. In Yemen, Himyar, Saba and Hadramawt fought for supremacy, and Aksum from Ethiopia intervened across the Red Sea. Central Arabian tribes like Kinda began to rise.
Arabia.12: Himyar conquered Saba around 275 and moved toward uniting all of Yemen. Arab client states formed on the empires' edges: the Lakhmids for Persia in Iraq. The Arabic language was developing, and caravan trade continued through oasis towns.
Arabia.13: Himyar ruled all of Yemen and extended influence into central Arabia. Its kings abandoned traditional gods for monotheism around 380, with many of the elite favoring Judaism, while Christianity spread in Najran. Early Arabic inscriptions appear on the northern fringes.
Arabia.14: Himyar dominated central Arabia through the Kinda tribal confederation. Arab client kingdoms, the Lakhmids for Persia and the Ghassanids for Byzantium, guarded the desert edges. Tradition says the Quraysh tribe settled Mecca, home of the Kaaba shrine, and Arabic poetry flourished.
Arabia.15: Himyar's Jewish king Dhu Nuwas massacred Christians at Najran c. 523, prompting an Aksumite invasion. The Aksumite general Abraha ruled Yemen, the Marib dam finally failed, and Persia took over Yemen around 570. Muhammad was born in Mecca c. 570, a trading town of the Quraysh.
Arabia.16: Muhammad began preaching in Mecca after his first revelation in 610 and moved to Medina in 622. He took Mecca in 630, and by his death in 632 Arabia was united under Islam. Arab armies conquered vast lands, and the capital moved to Damascus in 661.
Arabia.17: With the caliphs ruling from Damascus and later Baghdad, Arabia became a province, but Mecca and Medina drew ever more pilgrims and scholars, like Malik ibn Anas. Kharijite groups resisted the caliphs, and Oman developed its own Ibadi imamate around 750.
Arabia.18: Abbasid control weakened. Queen Zubayda funded a famous pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca, the Zaydi imamate was founded in Yemen in 897, and the radical Qarmatians took power in eastern Arabia around 899. Bedouin tribes remained largely independent.
Arabia.19: The Qarmatians shocked the Muslim world by sacking Mecca in 930 and carrying off the Black Stone, returning it in 951. Local dynasties ruled Yemen, and around the 960s the Sharifs, descendants of Muhammad, began ruling Mecca, an office they would hold for nearly a thousand years.
Arabia.20: The Sulayhid dynasty ruled Yemen, where Queen Arwa held power for decades. The Qarmatian state in eastern Arabia fell in 1077. Pilgrims and merchants continued to travel to Mecca, governed by its Sharifs under the nominal authority of the Fatimids or Abbasids.
Arabia.21: Saladin's Ayyubid dynasty conquered Yemen in 1174. The Crusader Reynald of Châtillon raided the Red Sea coast in 1182–83, threatening the holy cities. Pilgrims like Ibn Jubayr left vivid accounts of Mecca, and sea trade through Aden thrived.
Arabia.22: The Rasulid dynasty took over Yemen in 1229 and grew wealthy from Indian Ocean trade through Aden. The Mamluks of Egypt became protectors of Mecca and Medina. On the Gulf, the kingdom of Hormuz controlled shipping routes.
Arabia.23: Rasulid Yemen was a center of trade, farming and learning. Ibn Battuta visited Arabia, and Mansa Musa of Mali made a famous hajj in 1324. The Mamluks controlled the Hejaz, while Bedouin tribes dominated the interior.
Arabia.24: The Tahirids replaced the Rasulids in Yemen in 1454. Chinese fleets under Zheng He visited Aden and Hormuz. Arab navigators like Ahmad ibn Majid wrote guides to the Indian Ocean, and at the century's end Portuguese ships arrived in these waters.
Arabia.25: The Portuguese seized Muscat in 1507 and Hormuz in 1515 to control trade. The Ottomans took over the Hejaz in 1517 and Yemen later, while coffee from Yemen's port of Mocha spread across the Muslim world. Zaydi imams resisted the Ottomans in the highlands.
Arabia.26: Zaydi imams expelled the Ottomans from Yemen in 1635, and Mocha's coffee exports boomed. In Oman, the Ya'ariba dynasty drove the Portuguese out of Muscat in 1650 and built a maritime empire reaching East Africa. Ottoman Sharifs ruled Mecca.
Arabia.27: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab preached a strict return to early Islam, and in 1744 he allied with Muhammad ibn Saud of Diriyah, founding the First Saudi State. In Oman, the Al Bu Said dynasty took power, and Yemen's coffee monopoly faded as plantations rose elsewhere.
Arabia.28: The Saudi state expanded across Najd, taking Riyadh in 1773. On the Gulf coast, the Al Sabah family settled in Kuwait and the Al Khalifa took Bahrain in 1783. Britain's East India Company signed an agreement with Oman in 1798.
Arabia.29: Saudi forces sacked Karbala in 1802 and took Mecca and Medina, challenging the Ottomans. Egypt's Muhammad Ali sent armies that destroyed the First Saudi State and its capital Diriyah in 1818. Britain attacked Gulf sea raiders and imposed a maritime treaty in 1820.
Arabia.30: The Al Saud rebuilt a Second Saudi State from Riyadh, led by Faisal bin Turki. Britain seized Aden in 1839, and Egyptian troops withdrew from Arabia in 1840. Oman's sultan moved his court to Zanzibar, center of his East African trade.
Arabia.31: Gulf sheikhdoms signed a perpetual maritime truce with Britain in 1853, becoming the Trucial States. Oman and Zanzibar split in 1861. The Ottomans reoccupied al-Hasa and Yemen in the early 1870s, and the Suez Canal of 1869 made Aden a key port.
Arabia.32: The Rashidi dynasty of Ha'il defeated the Saudis in 1891, sending the Al Saud into exile in Kuwait. Britain signed exclusive treaties with Bahrain, the Trucial States and Kuwait, making them protectorates in all but name. Ottomans held the Hejaz and Yemen.
Arabia.33: Abdulaziz ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh in 1902 and began rebuilding his family's realm. The Hejaz Railway reached Medina in 1908, and Hussein became Sharif of Mecca that year. In Yemen, Imam Yahya fought Ottoman rule.
Arabia.34: Ibn Saud took al-Hasa from the Ottomans in 1913, backed by the Ikhwan religious militia. Sharif Hussein launched the Arab Revolt in 1916 with British support, helping drive the Ottomans out. Yemen under Imam Yahya became independent in 1918.
Arabia.35: Ibn Saud conquered Ha'il in 1921 and the Hejaz, with Mecca and Medina, in 1924–25, ending Hashemite rule there. When the Ikhwan rebelled against his limits on raiding, he crushed them by 1930. Pearl diving remained the Gulf's main industry.
Arabia.36: Ibn Saud proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932, the same year oil was found in Bahrain. Saudi Arabia fought a short war with Yemen in 1934. American geologists struck oil at Dammam in 1938, and Kuwait found oil that year too.
Arabia.37: Oil exports from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait grew rapidly after World War II, run by the American firm Aramco and British companies. President Roosevelt met Ibn Saud in 1945, beginning a lasting partnership. Imam Yahya of Yemen was assassinated in 1948.
Arabia.38: Oil money transformed Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, funding new cities, roads and schools. Saudi Arabia won a 50-50 profit share from Aramco in 1950. Ibn Saud died in 1953, and disputes over oases and borders flared across the Gulf.
Arabia.39: OPEC was founded in 1960, and Kuwait became independent in 1961. A 1962 revolution in North Yemen began a civil war in which Egypt and Saudi Arabia backed opposing sides. King Faisal took the Saudi throne in 1964, and South Yemen won independence from Britain in 1967.
Arabia.40: Sultan Qaboos took power in Oman in 1970, and the UAE, Qatar and Bahrain became independent in 1971. The 1973 Arab oil embargo quadrupled prices and brought huge wealth. King Faisal was assassinated in 1975, and militants seized Mecca's Grand Mosque in 1979.
Arabia.41: Gulf monarchies formed the Gulf Cooperation Council in 1981. They backed Iraq in the Iran-Iraq War, and tankers were attacked in the Gulf. Oil prices crashed in 1986, and Saudi Arabia helped fund Afghan fighters against the Soviets.
Arabia.42: North and South Yemen united in 1990. Iraq invaded Kuwait that year, and a US-led coalition expelled it in 1991, leaving American troops in Saudi Arabia, which Osama bin Laden opposed. Qatar launched Al Jazeera in 1996, and Dubai grew into a global hub.
Arabia.43: Fifteen of the 19 hijackers of September 11, 2001 were Saudi citizens, and al-Qaeda attacked inside Saudi Arabia in 2003–04. High oil prices funded rapid growth, especially in Dubai and Qatar. Yemen's government fought Houthi rebels in the north.
Arabia.44: Arab Spring protests in Bahrain were crushed in 2011, and Yemen's president Saleh was pushed out. Houthi rebels took Sanaa in 2014, and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015, causing a humanitarian disaster. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman launched sweeping social and economic changes.
Arabia.45: The UAE and Bahrain normalized ties with Israel in 2020, and Qatar hosted the 2022 World Cup. Saudi Arabia and Iran restored relations in 2023. Fighting in Yemen eased under a 2022 truce, but the Houthis attacked Red Sea shipping after the Gaza war began, drawing US and allied strikes.

Mesopotamia.0: Early farmers in northern Mesopotamia developed the Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf cultures. In the south, Ubaid villagers drained marshes and dug irrigation canals, building temples at Eridu. Uruk grew into one of the first true cities c. 4000–3100 BC, and cuneiform writing was invented c. 3200 BC.
Mesopotamia.1: Sumerian city-states such as Ur, Lagash and Uruk competed for land and water, each ruled by kings and devoted to patron gods. Sargon of Akkad built the first empire c. 2334 BC. Later, the Third Dynasty of Ur revived Sumer, and Ur-Nammu issued one of the earliest law codes c. 2100 BC.
Mesopotamia.2: Amorite kingdoms rose, and Hammurabi of Babylon united the south, issuing his famous code c. 1754 BC. The Hittites sacked Babylon in 1595 BC, after which the Kassites ruled it for centuries. In the north, Mitanni and then Assyria became great powers.
Mesopotamia.3: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, ruling from cities like Nimrud and Nineveh, dominated the Near East from 911 BC with a ruthless army and deportations. Ashurbanipal gathered a great library at Nineveh. Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC, ending Assyria.
Mesopotamia.4: Nebuchadnezzar II made Babylon the world's greatest city, building the Ishtar Gate and deporting Judeans there. His successor Nabonidus lost the city to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC. Under the Achaemenids, Babylon remained a rich royal capital and center of learning.
Mesopotamia.5: Babylonia was one of the Persian Empire's wealthiest satrapies. Revolts in 484 BC were crushed by Xerxes. Business families like the Murashu of Nippur managed land and taxes, and in 401 BC Greek mercenaries fought for a Persian prince at Cunaxa near Babylon.
Mesopotamia.6: Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BC and entered Babylon, planning to make it his capital, but he died there in 323 BC. His general Seleucus took the region and founded Seleucia on the Tigris c. 305 BC, which drew people away from Babylon.
Mesopotamia.7: Under the Seleucids, Seleucia on the Tigris became one of the largest Hellenistic cities. Babylon's temples still functioned, and scholars kept recording astronomy in cuneiform. The Babylonian priest Berossus wrote a history of his land in Greek.
Mesopotamia.8: The Parthians of Iran took Mesopotamia from the Seleucids in 141 BC. They built Ctesiphon across the Tigris from Seleucia, which became a royal residence. Small kingdoms like Characene near the Gulf grew rich on trade.
Mesopotamia.9: Parthian Mesopotamia was the frontier with Rome, and the Parthians crushed the Roman general Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC. Silk Road trade passed through, and local kingdoms such as Hatra, Adiabene and Osroene thrived under Parthian overlordship.
Mesopotamia.10: Under Parthian rule, Mesopotamia hosted a mix of Aramaic-speaking peoples, Greeks, Arabs and Jews. The royal family of Adiabene converted to Judaism. The last known cuneiform tablets were written around AD 75, ending a 3,000-year tradition.
Mesopotamia.11: Rome's Trajan captured Ctesiphon in 116, but Hadrian gave up the conquest. Roman armies sacked Seleucia in 165 and Ctesiphon in 198. The caravan city of Hatra withstood Roman sieges, and Jewish communities grew strong.
Mesopotamia.12: The Sasanians overthrew the Parthians in 224, ruling from Ctesiphon. The prophet Mani founded Manichaeism here, and Hatra was destroyed c. 240. Jewish academies at Sura and Pumbedita began the discussions later collected in the Babylonian Talmud.
Mesopotamia.13: Shapur II ruled Sasanian Persia for seventy years, fighting Rome along Mesopotamia's northern frontier. Roman emperor Julian invaded in 363 and died in retreat. Christians, increasingly seen as Roman sympathizers, faced periods of persecution. Rome ceded the fortress city of Nisibis to Persia after Julian's defeat.
Mesopotamia.14: The Church of the East organized itself at a council in Ctesiphon in 410 and spread eastward. Jewish scholars compiled the Babylonian Talmud. Late in the century the Mazdakite movement preached radical equality and briefly won royal support.
Mesopotamia.15: Khosrow I strengthened the Sasanian state, reforming taxes and building the great arched palace at Ctesiphon. The Lakhmid Arab kings at al-Hira guarded the desert frontier for Persia. Irrigated farmland in the south was among the most productive in the world.
Mesopotamia.16: Arab Muslim armies won at al-Qadisiyyah in 636 and took Ctesiphon, founding new garrison cities at Basra and Kufa. Iraq became a center of early Islamic politics, and the killing of Husayn at Karbala in 680 became a defining moment for Shia Islam.
Mesopotamia.17: Umayyad governors ruled Iraq firmly. The Abbasid revolution in 750 shifted the caliphate's center here, and in 762 Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad, which soon became one of the world's largest cities. Harun al-Rashid became caliph in 786.
Mesopotamia.18: Baghdad was a world center of trade and learning, where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works. The caliphs moved to Samarra for a time and relied on Turkish soldiers. The Zanj rebellion of enslaved workers in the south lasted from 869 to 883.
Mesopotamia.19: The caliphate weakened from debts, revolts and military coups. In 945 the Buyids, a Shia dynasty from Iran, took Baghdad, and the caliph became a figurehead. Baghdad remained a lively intellectual center despite political decline.
Mesopotamia.20: The Seljuk Turks entered Baghdad in 1055 and ruled as sultans in the caliph's name. Their vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya college in 1067, where al-Ghazali taught. Arab dynasties held Mosul and the countryside.
Mesopotamia.21: As Seljuk power broke up, the Zengids ruled Mosul and the caliphs regained real control of central Iraq. Caliph al-Nasir, from 1180, revived Abbasid authority and prestige. Baghdad was smaller than at its height but still important.
Mesopotamia.22: Abbasid Baghdad built the Mustansiriya college in 1233, but in 1258 the Mongols under Hulagu sacked the city, killing the caliph and many inhabitants. Iraq became a province of the Mongol Ilkhanate, ruled from Iran, and irrigation systems declined.
Mesopotamia.23: After the Ilkhanate collapsed in 1335, the Jalayirids ruled Baghdad. The Black Death struck. Timur sacked Baghdad in 1393 and again in 1401, and the population shrank as canals and farmland fell into ruin. Nomadic tribes gained ground in the countryside.
Mesopotamia.24: Turkmen confederations, first the Kara Koyunlu and then the Ak Koyunlu, ruled Iraq after Timur's devastation. Baghdad was a modest provincial city, and Bedouin and Kurdish tribes held much of the land. In 1508 the new Safavid dynasty of Iran took Baghdad.
Mesopotamia.25: The Safavids held Baghdad until Suleiman the Magnificent conquered it for the Ottomans in 1534, and Basra followed in 1546. Iraq became a frontier between Sunni Ottomans and Shia Safavids. Shrine cities like Najaf and Karbala drew pilgrims.
Mesopotamia.26: The Safavids under Shah Abbas retook Baghdad in 1623, but the Ottomans regained it in 1638. The 1639 Treaty of Zuhab set a frontier that roughly survives today as the Iran-Iraq border. Local families controlled Basra and many tribes were self-governing.
Mesopotamia.27: Hasan Pasha and his son Ahmad Pasha governed Baghdad, founding a line of semi-independent rulers drawn from their household of Georgian mamluks. Nader Shah of Iran besieged Baghdad in 1733 and Mosul in 1743 but failed to conquer them.
Mesopotamia.28: Georgian mamluk pashas governed Baghdad with little interference from Istanbul. Persia occupied Basra in 1776–79. Under Büyük Sulayman Pasha from 1780, order improved, and the British East India Company set up a residency at Basra.
Mesopotamia.29: Wahhabi raiders from Arabia sacked Karbala in 1802. The mamluk governor Dawud Pasha, from 1817, built an army and schools and expanded trade. Kurdish emirates such as Baban held power in the north, and British trade at Basra kept growing.
Mesopotamia.30: In 1831 plague and floods devastated Baghdad, and the Ottomans used the moment to end mamluk rule and govern directly. They suppressed the Kurdish emirates in the following years. The 1847 Treaty of Erzurum tried to settle the border with Iran.
Mesopotamia.31: Governor Midhat Pasha, 1869–72, introduced land registration, schools, a printing press and a tramway, pushing tribes to settle and farm. British steamers on the Tigris and the opening of the Suez Canal tied Iraq more closely to world trade.
Mesopotamia.32: Iraq was divided into the Ottoman provinces of Mosul, Baghdad and Basra. Many southern tribes, settling as farmers, adopted Shia Islam. British commercial influence grew, and Germany began seeking a railway concession to Baghdad. Ottoman schools trained a new generation of Iraqi officers and officials.
Mesopotamia.33: Germany won the Baghdad Railway concession in 1903. The 1908 Young Turk Revolution brought elections but also stronger Turkish centralization, and some Iraqi officers and intellectuals joined Arab nationalist groups. Foreign companies began competing for rights to the region's suspected oil.
Mesopotamia.34: Britain invaded in 1914 to protect its oil interests, suffered a major defeat at Kut in 1916, then took Baghdad in 1917 and Mosul in 1918. The war brought hunger and disease to Iraqis, and Britain set up direct military administration, angering many who had hoped for self-rule.
Mesopotamia.35: A large revolt against British rule in 1920 was suppressed, and Britain created the Kingdom of Iraq under Faisal I in 1921 within a League of Nations mandate. Mosul was confirmed as part of Iraq in 1926, and oil was struck near Kirkuk in 1927.
Mesopotamia.36: Iraq became independent in 1932, though Britain kept bases and oil interests. The army massacred Assyrians at Simele in 1933, King Faisal died that year, and in 1936 Iraq saw the Arab world's first military coup.
Mesopotamia.37: A pro-Axis coup in 1941 led to a British invasion and the Farhud, a deadly attack on Baghdad's Jews. Protests in 1948 overturned a new treaty with Britain, and Iraq fought in the 1948 Arab-Israeli war.
Mesopotamia.38: Most of Iraq's ancient Jewish community left in 1950–51. Oil income funded development projects, and Iraq joined the pro-Western Baghdad Pact in 1955. In 1958 army officers overthrew and killed the royal family, and Abd al-Karim Qasim took power.
Mesopotamia.39: The Ba'ath Party killed Qasim in a 1963 coup, but was soon pushed out, and returned in 1968, with Saddam Hussein rising behind President al-Bakr. Kurdish forces under Mustafa Barzani fought the government in the north.
Mesopotamia.40: Iraq nationalized its oil in 1972 and used rising revenues for roads, schools and hospitals. A Kurdish revolt collapsed in 1975 after Iran ended its support. In 1979 Saddam Hussein became president and purged rivals.
Mesopotamia.41: Saddam invaded Iran in 1980, starting an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands. In the Anfal campaign against the Kurds, his forces used chemical weapons, killing about 5,000 at Halabja in 1988. Iraq ended the war deeply in debt.
Mesopotamia.42: Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 and was expelled by a US-led coalition in 1991. Uprisings by Shia and Kurds were crushed, but the Kurds gained self-rule under a no-fly zone. Harsh UN sanctions impoverished ordinary Iraqis.
Mesopotamia.43: A US-led invasion toppled Saddam Hussein in 2003. An insurgency and sectarian civil war killed tens of thousands of civilians, peaking in 2006–07. Iraqis voted on a new constitution in 2005, and Saddam was executed in 2006.
Mesopotamia.44: US troops left in 2011, and sectarian tensions grew. ISIS seized Mosul in 2014 and committed genocide against the Yazidis before Iraqi and Kurdish forces, with international help, defeated it by 2017. Mass protests against corruption erupted in 2019.
Mesopotamia.45: A US strike killed Iranian general Qasem Soleimani in Baghdad in 2020. Iraq experienced relative stability under governments balancing ties with Iran and the US, funded by oil. Corruption, unemployment, and severe drought and water shortages remained major challenges.

Persia.0: In the Zagros Mountains, people at sites like Ganj Dareh were among the first to herd goats, c. 8000 BC. Farming villages spread across the Iranian plateau, making painted pottery at sites like Tepe Sialk. Susa was founded c. 4200 BC, and Proto-Elamite writing appeared near the end of the period.
Persia.1: Elam, centered on Susa and Anshan in southwest Iran, was a major civilization that alternately traded and fought with Mesopotamia. Eastern Iran had its own urban cultures, such as Shahr-i Sokhta and the Jiroft culture. Elamites helped bring down the Sumerian city of Ur c. 2004 BC.
Persia.2: Elamite kings ruled from Susa, and Untash-Napirisha built the great ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil c. 1250 BC. Shutruk-Nakhunte raided Babylon c. 1158 BC, carrying off Hammurabi's law stele. Indo-Iranian speaking peoples moved onto the plateau, and Zoroaster may have lived in this era, though his dates are debated.
Persia.3: Iranian peoples, the Medes and Persians, settled western Iran and spread Zoroastrian belief. Assyria campaigned in the Zagros and sacked Susa c. 646 BC, weakening Elam. The Medes grew strong and, with Babylon, destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC.
Persia.4: Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire in 550 BC, conquering Media, Lydia and Babylon. His son Cambyses took Egypt in 525 BC. Darius I, from 522 BC, organized the empire into satrapies, built the Royal Road and began Persepolis, creating the largest empire yet seen.
Persia.5: Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BC but was defeated at Salamis and Plataea. The Persian Empire nevertheless remained vast and wealthy, using Aramaic in administration and tolerating local religions. Persepolis was completed as a ceremonial capital.
Persia.6: Persia remained powerful, reconquering Egypt in 343 BC, but palace murders weakened the throne. Alexander the Great conquered the empire in 334–330 BC, defeated Darius III and burned Persepolis. After his death the Seleucids ruled Iran from 312 BC.
Persia.7: Seleucid control over Iran slipped. Bactria in the northeast broke away c. 250 BC, and in 247 BC the Parni nomads founded the Parthian or Arsacid kingdom. Antiochus III marched east in 209 BC to reassert power, but the Parthians endured.
Persia.8: The Parthian king Mithridates I conquered the Iranian plateau and took Mesopotamia in 141 BC. Parthia traded with Han China along the Silk Road but faced dangerous nomad invasions from the east. Mithridates II restored Parthian strength late in the century.
Persia.9: Parthian horse archers crushed the Roman general Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC, establishing Parthia as Rome's great eastern rival. They raided Syria in 40 BC and defeated Mark Antony's invasion in 36 BC. Parthian kings ruled through powerful noble families.
Persia.10: Parthian kings like Vologases I balanced Rome by sharing influence over Armenia after the Treaty of Rhandeia in 63. Silk Road trade enriched the empire, though rival claimants often fought for the throne. Zoroastrian traditions were preserved and promoted.
Persia.11: Trajan invaded and took Ctesiphon in 116, and later Roman armies sacked Mesopotamian cities in the 160s and 190s. Weakened by these wars and internal revolts, the Parthian state declined. The Kushan Empire dominated lands to the east.
Persia.12: Ardashir I overthrew the Parthians and founded the Sasanian Empire in 224, centralizing power and promoting Zoroastrianism. His son Shapur I defeated Rome and captured Emperor Valerian in 260, celebrated in rock reliefs. The prophet Mani preached his new religion at court.
Persia.13: Shapur II ruled for about seventy years, fighting Rome and repelling Julian's invasion in 363. Armenia was divided between Rome and Persia c. 387. Christians in the empire were sometimes persecuted as potential allies of Christian Rome.
Persia.14: Sasanian kings like Bahram V faced the Hephthalites, nomads from Central Asia who killed King Peroz in 484 and demanded tribute. Kavad I briefly backed the Mazdakite movement, which preached sharing property, causing social upheaval.
Persia.15: Khosrow I, 531–579, the high point of Sasanian Persia, reformed taxes and the army, crushed the Mazdakites and built palaces. Scholars translated Greek and Indian works, and chess arrived from India. Persia fought Justinian's Byzantium and extended its reach to Yemen.
Persia.16: Khosrow II's war against Byzantium in 602–628 exhausted both empires. Arab Muslim armies then won at al-Qadisiyyah and Nahavand, and the death of Yazdegerd III in 651 ended the Sasanian Empire. Iran came under the caliphate, and Islam spread slowly.
Persia.17: Iran was ruled by Umayyad governors, and many Zoroastrians gradually converted to Islam, while some migrated to India as the Parsis. The Abbasid revolution began in Khorasan in 747, and Persians, such as the Barmakid family, gained great influence at the Abbasid court.
Persia.18: As Abbasid control weakened, Iranian dynasties rose: the Tahirids, Saffarids and Samanids. New Persian emerged as a literary language written in Arabic script, and the poet Rudaki wrote at the Samanid court. Scholars like the physician al-Razi made Iran a center of learning.
Persia.19: The Samanids of Bukhara patronized Persian culture, and Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh. The Buyids, a Shia dynasty from northern Iran, ruled the west and took Baghdad in 945. The Ghaznavids rose in the east, and Ibn Sina was born in 980.
Persia.20: Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh c. 1010, and Ibn Sina wrote his medical and philosophical works. Seljuk Turks conquered Persia in the 1040s, ruling with Persian administrators like vizier Nizam al-Mulk. Omar Khayyam reformed the calendar, and the Assassins seized Alamut in 1090.
Persia.21: Seljuk power declined after Sultan Sanjar, and the Khwarazmshahs took over much of Iran. The Ismaili Assassins held mountain fortresses. Persian poetry flourished with Nizami and Attar. Fertile cities like Nishapur and Merv were rich trading centers, unaware of the Mongol storm to come.
Persia.22: The Mongols devastated Persia in 1219–21, destroying cities and killing vast numbers. Hulagu destroyed the Assassins and founded the Ilkhanate in 1256. Nasir al-Din Tusi built an observatory at Maragheh, poets like Saadi wrote in Shiraz, and the Ilkhan Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295.
Persia.23: Ghazan's reforms and Rashid al-Din's world history marked the Ilkhanate's height, but it collapsed in 1335. Local dynasties like the Muzaffarids ruled, and Hafez wrote poetry in Shiraz. In the 1380s Timur conquered Persia with great brutality.
Persia.24: Timur's son Shah Rukh ruled eastern Iran from Herat, sponsoring art and architecture. Turkmen confederations, the Kara Koyunlu and then Ak Koyunlu, ruled western Iran. The Safavid Sufi order of Ardabil built a militant following.
Persia.25: Shah Ismail founded the Safavid dynasty in 1501 and made Shia Islam the state religion, converting most of Iran over time. The Ottomans defeated him at Chaldiran in 1514. Shah Tahmasp held off Ottomans and Uzbeks, and Abbas I took the throne in 1588.
Persia.26: Shah Abbas I, 1588–1629, rebuilt the army, retook lands from the Ottomans and seized Hormuz from Portugal. He made Isfahan a magnificent capital with grand mosques and squares. Silk trade with Europe prospered, but later shahs were weaker.
Persia.27: Afghan invaders took Isfahan in 1722, ending effective Safavid rule. Nader Shah drove them out, crowned himself in 1736 and sacked Delhi in 1739, carrying off the Peacock Throne. After his assassination in 1747, Iran fell into civil war.
Persia.28: Karim Khan Zand ruled most of Iran from Shiraz, 1751–79, bringing peace. After his death the Qajar chief Agha Mohammad Khan fought his way to power, made Tehran his capital in 1786, sacked Tbilisi in 1795 and was crowned in 1796.
Persia.29: Fath Ali Shah ruled Qajar Iran, presiding over an elaborate court. Iran lost Georgia and other Caucasus lands to Russia in the war of 1804–13. Britain and France competed for influence in Tehran, and a second war with Russia broke out in 1826.
Persia.30: Russia defeated Iran again, and the 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay took more Caucasus land and imposed trade privileges. Iranian sieges of Herat in 1837–38 failed. In 1844 the Báb started a new religious movement, and Naser al-Din Shah took the throne in 1848.
Persia.31: Chief minister Amir Kabir founded the Dar ul-Funun college before his execution in 1852, and Bábis were persecuted, giving rise to the Bahá'í Faith. Britain defeated Iran in 1856–57 over Herat. A severe famine in 1870–72 killed many people.
Persia.32: Britain and Russia competed for influence as Naser al-Din Shah sold concessions to foreigners. The Tobacco Protest of 1891–92, backed by Shia clerics, forced him to cancel a British tobacco monopoly. He was assassinated in 1896.
Persia.33: Iranians launched the Constitutional Revolution in 1905, winning a parliament in 1906. Britain and Russia divided Iran into spheres of influence in 1907. The shah bombarded parliament in 1908, the year oil was discovered in the southwest.
Persia.34: Russian pressure ended the Constitutional Revolution in 1911. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company began exporting oil. Though neutral in World War I, Iran was occupied by foreign armies and struck by a terrible famine in 1917–19.
Persia.35: Reza Khan took power in a 1921 coup and founded the Pahlavi dynasty in 1925. He built a modern army, centralized the state, created secular courts and schools, and began the Trans-Iranian Railway in 1927. Nomadic tribes were forcibly settled, and the clergy lost influence.
Persia.36: Reza Shah officially asked foreign governments to call the country Iran in 1935. He banned the veil in 1936 and harshly suppressed opposition, while the Trans-Iranian Railway was finished in 1938. Iran developed trade ties with Germany.
Persia.37: Britain and the Soviet Union invaded in 1941 and forced Reza Shah to abdicate in favor of his son Mohammad Reza. The Allied leaders met at the Tehran Conference in 1943. After the war, Soviet-backed separatists in Azerbaijan were removed in 1946.
Persia.38: Prime Minister Mosaddegh nationalized Iran's oil in 1951, but a US and British-backed coup ousted him in 1953. The shah then ruled with growing power, supported by the United States and the SAVAK secret police, created in 1957.
Persia.39: The shah's White Revolution of 1963 brought land reform and votes for women. Ayatollah Khomeini denounced the shah and was exiled in 1964. Oil revenues grew, and the economy modernized rapidly as cities grew. Political parties were tightly controlled, and resentment of the shah's rule spread quietly.
Persia.40: The oil boom of 1973 brought rapid wealth along with inflation and inequality. Mass protests in 1978 forced the shah to leave, and in 1979 the Islamic Revolution created an Islamic Republic led by Khomeini. Students seized the US embassy, holding hostages for 444 days.
Persia.41: The Iran-Iraq War of 1980–88 killed hundreds of thousands. The new government suppressed opposition, executing thousands of prisoners in 1988. Khomeini died in 1989, and Ali Khamenei became Supreme Leader. The Islamic Republic's institutions, including the Revolutionary Guards, grew in power.
Persia.42: President Rafsanjani focused on rebuilding the economy after the war. Reformist Mohammad Khatami won the 1997 election, promising greater openness, but hardliners resisted, closing newspapers, and student protests in 1999 were crushed. A young population pushed for social change.
Persia.43: Iran's nuclear program came to international attention in 2002, leading to sanctions. Hardliner Mahmoud Ahmadinejad became president in 2005. His disputed 2009 reelection sparked the mass Green Movement protests, which were suppressed. The economy suffered from sanctions and mismanagement.
Persia.44: Sanctions hurt the economy. President Rouhani agreed to the JCPOA nuclear deal in 2015, but the US withdrew in 2018. Iran expanded its influence in Syria, Iraq and beyond, and protests over economic hardship erupted in 2017–18 and 2019.
Persia.45: The death of Mahsa Amini in custody sparked the 'Woman, Life, Freedom' protests in 2022, met with a harsh crackdown. Iran and Israel exchanged direct strikes in 2024, and in June 2025 a 12-day war with Israel ended with US strikes on nuclear sites.
